cards.explanation: The answer is God Himself. The writer says, “As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God.” (Psalm 42:1). He isn't longing for something God hands out. He's longing for God. Think of me staring at the oven window while a batch bakes, except his longing is aimed at the best possible target.

The answer is False. The writer's question does not show he is already standing in God's presence. He asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (Psalm 42:2). That's a question about a time to come, and the verse doesn't say he's already there. I think the thirst in that verse is something he feels strongly.

The answer is “Where is your God?” While he cries, men ask him that all day long (Psalm 42:3). It comes back later, when his enemies taunt him “…all day long…” with the very same question (Psalm 42:10). Same question, twice, friends, and it never takes a day off.

The answer is full of shouts of joy and praise. He remembers leading the festive procession to the house of God “…with shouts of joy and praise.” (Psalm 42:4). Shouts, friends! That's a crowd with its whole voice turned on. I think remembering a day like that hits hard when your tears are your food now.

The answer is hope. The writer tells his soul, “Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence.” (Psalm 42:5). Notice he doesn't say the soul feels better yet. He says to aim it at God and keep going. That's a solid talking-to.

The answer is remembers. The writer says, “…my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon…” (Psalm 42:6). Look at that word “Therefore.” The despair is tied right to the remembering, friends. He tells God he remembers Him instead of letting go.

The answer is True. The writer says, “Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me.” (Psalm 42:7). Your waterfalls, Your breakers, Your waves. It's a picture of how heavy it all feels, and he's telling God whose waves they are.

The answer is the LORD's song. The verse says, “The LORD decrees His loving devotion by day, and at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life.” (Psalm 42:8). Day has devotion, night has a song. Even in the dark, bakers, he isn't left without something with him.

The answer is forgotten. The writer says to God, “Why have You forgotten me?” (Psalm 42:9). That's his honest question, said straight to God, whom he has just called “my Rock.” I think it takes real trust to bring a question that hard right to Him.

The answer is “My Savior and my God.” The writer says, “Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.” (Psalm 42:11). The first time he told his soul to hope, he didn't add that. This time he calls God his Savior. It's a good line to hold on to, friends.

The answer is deceitful and unjust men. The writer of Psalm 43 prays, “deliver me from deceitful and unjust men.” (Psalm 43:1). Right alongside it, he asks God to plead his case against an ungodly nation. He's naming exactly what he needs help with, and I say that's a good way to pray.

The answer is the God of my refuge. The writer says, “For You are the God of my refuge. Why have You rejected me?” (Psalm 43:2). He says who God is to him, and then he asks the hard question anyway. Both are in the same breath, friends.

The answer is to lead him to where God dwells. The writer prays, “Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain and to the place where You dwell.” (Psalm 43:3). Light and truth are the guides, and God's dwelling place is the destination. Sounds like the best set of directions you could ask for.

The answer is joy. The writer says he will go “…to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy.” (Psalm 43:4). Not just a joy, but his GREATEST joy. When a man with tears for food says that, I believe him.

The answer is False. The writer does not say he will stay silent at the altar. He says, “I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God.” (Psalm 43:4). That's praise with sound, strings and all. I think he's planning something good.
The answer is the harp. The writer says, “I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God.” (Psalm 43:4). He's got the instrument picked out already, friends. That's a man who is planning on praising.
